etymology: Hebrew Kesalon, perhaps “hope” or “confidence,” a place on the northern border of Judah identified with mount Jearim.
biblical_def: Chesalon was a place named in the marking out of the north border of the tribe of Judah, where the border “passed along unto the side of mount Jearim, which is Chesalon, on the north side” (Jos 15:10). Thus Chesalon and mount Jearim were one, a height in the hill country that served as a fixed landmark along the line dividing Judah from Benjamin and Dan. The border ran from Baalah westward, compassing toward mount Seir, passing along the side of mount Jearim, and so going down to Bethshemesh. The naming of Chesalon belongs to the great work of Joshua in which the LORD apportioned the land by lot among the tribes, that each should know the bounds of his inheritance and hold it as a gift from the hand of God. No story of war or wonder is told of Chesalon; it is a quiet name among the borders, a stone in the wall of Judah’s allotment. Yet the very exactness of the record, naming hill and side and direction, witnesses to the faithfulness of God in giving Israel the land He had sworn to their fathers, measuring out to each tribe its portion with a precision that left nothing to chance.
webster_summary: A place on the north border of Judah, identified with mount Jearim, marking the line toward Benjamin and Dan.

etymology: Hebrew Beth-ha-Arabah, “house of the desert” or “house of the Arabah,” a town on the border of Judah and Benjamin.
biblical_def: Beth-arabah, the “house of the desert” or “house of the Arabah,” was a town in the wilderness region descending toward the Jordan and the Salt Sea, lying upon the line that divided Judah from Benjamin. It is named among the cities of Judah in the wilderness (Jos 15:61), and again as a point on Judah’s north border, where “the border went up to Beth-hogla, and passed along by the north of Beth-arabah” (Jos 15:6). When the lot of Benjamin came up, Beth-arabah is reckoned among its cities as well (Jos 18:22), for it stood upon the very boundary between the two tribes. Its name speaks of its place in the Arabah, the deep rift of desert that runs down to the Dead Sea, a barren and forsaken-seeming tract; yet even here the LORD planted the inheritance of His people and named the towns of His allotment. Beth-arabah is a witness that no corner of the land was too lowly or too waste to be numbered in the portion God gave Israel. The wilderness town, set on the border of two tribes, was reckoned by name in the dividing of the land, that the people might possess in full the inheritance promised to their fathers.

etymology: Hebrew Tsela, perhaps “a rib” or “a side,” a town of Benjamin, the burying-place of the house of Kish.
biblical_def: Zelah was a town in the allotment of the tribe of Benjamin, numbered among its cities in the dividing of the land (Jos 18:28). Its chief renown in Scripture is as the burying-place of the house of Kish, the family of King Saul. When David had delivered the bones of Saul and of Jonathan his son out of the hands of the men of Jabesh-gilead, “the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son buried they in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father” (2Sa 21:14). So the first king of Israel, after his long unraveling and his death upon Gilboa, was laid at last in his own father’s tomb among his own tribe, and Jonathan his beloved son with him. The burying of Saul in Zelah closed the troubled story of the house that the LORD had set aside, and after it was done, “God was intreated for the land.” Zelah thus stands as a quiet grave at the end of a fallen dynasty, a town of Benjamin holding the dust of the king whom God had rejected for his disobedience. It is a sober witness that the proudest house comes down at last to a sepulchre, and that the kingdom is the LORD’s to give and to take away.

etymology: Hebrew Motsah, perhaps “a going forth” or “a spring,” a town in the allotment of Benjamin.
biblical_def: Mozah was a town numbered among the cities of the tribe of Benjamin in the dividing of the land (Jos 18:26). It stands in the list with Mizpeh, Chephirah, Rekem, Irpeel, and Taralah, the towns set apart for Benjamin between Judah and the children of Joseph. No event of Scripture is recorded at Mozah; it is one of the many quiet names that fill out the catalogue of Benjamin’s inheritance, a town that the people knew and dwelt in, though no story attaches to it. Yet its silent place in the record is not without weight. The LORD, who apportioned the land by lot, caused even the least of these towns to be written down by name, that the bounds of every tribe and the dwelling of every family might be known and held secure. Mozah was as truly Benjamin’s as Bethel or Gibeon; the smallest town in the allotment was a real gift of God, a place where households of Israel lived under His covenant and worshipped Him in the land He had given. Mozah is a witness that the faithfulness of God reaches down to the least and most obscure of His people’s portions, and that nothing in His gift is forgotten or unnamed.

etymology: Hebrew Qeriyoth, “cities” or “towns” (a plural form), the name of Kerioth-hezron among the southernmost towns of Judah.
biblical_def: Kerioth, or Kerioth-hezron, was a town reckoned among the uttermost cities of the tribe of Judah, toward the border of Edom in the south (Jos 15:25). It stands in the long catalogue of Judah’s southern towns, in the dry and difficult country of the Negeb, far from the watered heart of the land. The name itself, a plural form meaning “cities” or “towns,” suited a cluster of settlements in that arid region. Like its fellow towns of the south, Kerioth was a real possession of Judah, a place where the people of God dwelt at the edge of the wilderness, holding the bounds of the inheritance the LORD had given them by lot. Some have linked the name of Kerioth to the surname of Judas Iscariot, taking “Iscariot” as “man of Kerioth”; this is an old tradition and no more, not asserted by the Scripture, which nowhere names the betrayer’s town. Kerioth itself remains simply one of the southern cities of Judah, named in the allotment that the people might know and possess the southern reaches of their land. It is a witness that the LORD gave to Judah even the hard and far-off country of the south, that the whole inheritance might be held as His faithful gift.

etymology: Hebrew Beth-Anath, “house of Anath” (a heathen goddess), a fortified town in the allotment of Naphtali.
biblical_def: Beth-anath was a fortified town in the allotment of the tribe of Naphtali, named among its fenced cities in the dividing of the land (Jos 19:38). Its name, “house of Anath,” recalls a heathen Canaanite goddess once honoured there, a mark of the idolatry that filled the land before Israel came. When Naphtali received its inheritance, it did not drive out the Canaanites who dwelt in Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh, “but he dwelt among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land: nevertheless the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and of Beth-anath became tributaries unto them” (Jud 1:33). So Naphtali fell short of the full obedience God commanded, which was to dispossess the heathen utterly; instead the tribe suffered the Canaanites to remain, content to make them tributaries rather than to cast them out. This incomplete obedience left the snares of idolatry within the land, a root of later apostasy. Beth-anath thus stands as a sober witness against half-hearted obedience. The LORD had commanded the full purging of the land from its idols and its peoples; Naphtali settled for less, and the heathen the tribe spared became a thorn in its side. The town whose very name honoured a false goddess was left standing, and with it the old temptation to forsake the LORD.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the warning against incomplete obedience. Naphtali did not drive out the Canaanites of Beth-anath as the LORD had commanded, but suffered them to remain and made them tributaries instead. This half-hearted obedience left the snares of idolatry within the land; the town whose very name honoured a false goddess was spared, and with it the old temptation to forsake the LORD. To obey God by halves is to leave a thorn in the side that festers into later apostasy.

The Canaanites Naphtali spared became, as God had foretold, thorns in their sides and their gods a snare. The lesson is plain for every age: sin tolerated is sin that strengthens. What the LORD commands to be wholly put away must not be merely subdued and kept about as a tributary; the half-measure that leaves the idol standing is no obedience at all, but a slow surrender. Beth-anath is a monument to the cost of doing the LORD’s work by halves.

etymology: Hebrew Helqath, “a portion” or “a smooth field,” a Levitical city in the allotment of Asher.
biblical_def: Helkath was a town in the allotment of the tribe of Asher, named among its border cities in the dividing of the land (Jos 19:25). When the Levites received their cities scattered among the tribes, Helkath was given out of Asher to the children of Gershon, the Levitical family, with its suburbs for their cattle (Jos 21:31). So this town of Asher became a Levitical city, a dwelling for the servants of the LORD set in the midst of the tribe, that the worship and teaching of God might be near to the people of that region. The Levites had no land-inheritance of their own among their brethren, for the LORD was their portion; instead they were given cities throughout all the tribes, that the knowledge of God might be spread abroad and no part of Israel be left without the ministry of His worship. Helkath, whose name means “a portion” or “a smooth field,” was one such dwelling of the Levites in the far north of the land. It stands as a witness to the wisdom of God in scattering the Levites among the tribes, so that the law and the worship of the LORD were never far from any of His people, but a teaching house of God was set within their own borders.

etymology: Hebrew Mishal, perhaps “entreaty” or “a hollow,” a Levitical city in the allotment of Asher.
biblical_def: Mishal was a town in the allotment of the tribe of Asher, named among its cities in the dividing of the land (Jos 19:26). When the Levites received their cities throughout the tribes, Mishal was given out of Asher to the children of Gershon, the Levitical family, with its suburbs (Jos 21:30). So this town of the northern coastland became a Levitical city, a dwelling for the servants of the LORD among the people of Asher, that the worship and the teaching of God might be set within their borders. The Levites, having no land-inheritance of their own, were planted by the LORD’s appointment in cities throughout all Israel, so that no tribe, however far to the north or the sea, should be without the ministry of God’s house among them. Mishal stands beside Helkath, Abdon, and Rehob as one of the four Levitical cities given out of Asher to the Gershonites. It is a witness to the same gracious order: that the LORD spread His worship through every region of His people’s land, scattering the Levites as lamps through Israel, that the knowledge of God might shine in the remotest corners, and the people near the sea be as well taught in His law as those who dwelt nearest the tabernacle.

That the people near the sea should be as well taught in God’s law as those nearest the tabernacle commends the even care of the LORD for all His people. He did not leave the remote tribes to dwell in ignorance while the centre flourished; He set His Levites in Asher as in Judah, that the light of His word might shine in every corner. The scattering of these cities is a standing witness that the knowledge of God is meant for the whole of His people, to the uttermost border.

biblical_def: Kishion was a town in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar, named among its cities in the dividing of the land (Jos 19:20). When the Levites received their cities scattered through the tribes, Kishion was given out of Issachar to the children of Gershon, the Levitical family, with its suburbs (Jos 21:28). So this town of Issachar, in the rich plain country between Carmel and the Jordan, became a Levitical city, a dwelling for the servants of the LORD among the people of that tribe, that the worship and the teaching of God might be near to them. Issachar was the tribe of which the men of understanding had knowledge of the times, to know what Israel ought to do; and the planting of a Levitical city in their midst was part of that gracious provision by which the law of God was kept near to His people. The Levites, having no inheritance of land, for the LORD was their portion, were given Kishion and its like throughout Israel, that no tribe should lack the ministry of His house. Kishion stands as one witness among many to the wisdom of God in scattering the Levitical towns, so that the worship of the LORD was set within the borders of every tribe and the light of His word shone in the plain of Issachar as in the hill country of Judah.

etymology: Hebrew En-Gannim, “spring of gardens” or “fountain of gardens,” a Levitical city in the allotment of Issachar.
biblical_def: En-gannim, the “spring of gardens,” was a town in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar, named among its cities in the dividing of the land (Jos 19:21). Its name speaks of a well-watered place, a fountain among gardens in the fruitful plain that fell to Issachar. When the Levites received their cities throughout the tribes, En-gannim was given out of Issachar to the children of Gershon, the Levitical family, with its suburbs (Jos 21:29). So this fair and fruitful town became a Levitical city, a dwelling for the servants of the LORD among the people of Issachar, that the worship and teaching of God might be near to them. The Levites, who had no land-inheritance of their own, for the LORD was their portion, were planted by His appointment in cities throughout all Israel, that no tribe should be without the ministry of His house. En-gannim, a spring of gardens, becomes a fitting figure of the Levitical city: for as a fountain waters the gardens about it and makes them flourish, so the worship and the word of God, set in the midst of a tribe, water the souls of the people and make them fruitful unto the LORD. It is a witness to the wisdom of God, who scattered His worship through every region of His people’s land.
